newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agriculture dept holds civil rights meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agriculture dept holds civil rights meeting.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department, which has been called the "last plantation" because of alleged racial discrimination, on Wednesday held a day-long town meeting on civil rights.

Department employees, farmers and others gave emotional testimonials before top agriculture officials in an unprecedented session hosted by Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and lasting more than seven hours.
"Racism has raised its ugly head in this department for too long," a department employee told the crowded auditorium.

An elderly African-American farmer, his body quivering with emotion, said he had sent his daughters to college but could not fulfill his sons' dreams of joining him on the land as it was too hard to get "start up" help from the government.
"I'm a fourth-generation black farmer and I'm about to lose the land that my great grandfather acquired because of discrimination," another told the secretary.

Black farmers have complained they suffer discrimination in Agriculture Department lending programs and that racism was the basis for loan rejections and foreclosures. They also say loan discrimination is a major reason why the number of black farms has dwindled more rapidly than the overall U.S. figure.

Last month, Glickman formed an action team to do a civil rights audit of the department and halted pending foreclosure sales until they could be reviewed for discrimination or inconsistency in program delivery.

"We have a real opportunity to make positive changes in the area of structure in this department as well as civil rights enforcement and to ensure that both our employees and our customers are treated fairly and with dignity," Glickman said at the start of Wednesday's session.
He said the civil rights team would produce a report with recommendations within the next 30 days.
"We will not let this report gather dust. We will make necessary changes to make sure that USDA is the leader in human relations in the government," Glickman said.
The farmers' charges followed long-standing accusations of discrimination within the department.
Throughout the mammoth agency, which occupies two office buildings, workers clustered around in-house television sets watching the meeting.
"People have really unloaded what's on their minds," said Paul Johnson, a top department manager who chaired the session. "For too long things have been bottled up."
